content: The classical definition of probability is closely associated with the works of Pierre-Simon Laplace. In his Théorie analytique des probabilités, Laplace articulated this definition as a direct consequence of the principle of indifference. According to this principle, if elementary events are assigned equal probabilities, the probability of a disjunction of elementary events is calculated as the number of events in the disjunction divided by the total number of elementary events. This classical definition of probability faced criticism from several 19th-century scholars, including John Venn and George Boole. However, it experienced a resurgence of interest due to the growing focus on Bayesian probability. Historically, the mathematical study of probability emerged relatively late compared to other fields like geometry, despite evidence of humans engaging in games of chance, such as dice, in prehistoric times across various cultures. The exact year of its formal inception is known: in 1654, Blaise Pascal corresponded with Pierre de Fermat regarding two problems related to games of chance. These problems were brought to Pascal's attention by Chevalier de Méré, whom Pascal had accompanied on a trip earlier that year. One of the problems, known as the problem of points, was a classic issue that had been addressed as early as 1494 by Luca Pacioli. It dealt with the fair division of stakes when a game is interrupted before its conclusion. The other problem involved a mathematical rule of thumb that appeared to fail when extending a dice game from one die to two dice. This latter problem, or paradox, was discovered by de Méré himself and, according to him, demonstrated the risks of applying mathematics to real-world scenarios. During their discussions, Pascal and de Méré also explored other mathematical and philosophical issues. De Méré believed these discussions reinforced his philosophical view that mathematics, while beautiful, perfect, and flawless, was poorly connected to the imperfect reality of the world and often impractical. Pascal, as a mathematician, was provoked by de Méré's ideas and became determined to refute them by solving the two problems purely through mathematics. He succeeded in doing so. When Pascal learned that Fermat, already a distinguished mathematician, had independently arrived at the same solutions using different methods, he was convinced that they had conclusively resolved the problems. Their correspondence circulated among other scholars of the time and marked the beginning of widespread mathematical interest in problems arising from games of chance. However, this does not imply that Pascal and Fermat had a clear and comprehensive concept of probability, nor that they made the first accurate calculations regarding games of chance. For instance, no clear distinction was yet made between probabilities and expected values. The first individual to recognize the necessity of a precise definition of probability was Laplace. As late as 1814, he stated: The theory of chance consists in reducing all events of the same kind to a certain number of equally possible cases, that is, to such cases as we may be equally undecided about regarding their existence, and in determining the number of cases favorable to the event whose probability is sought. The ratio of this number to that of all possible cases is the measure of this probability, which is thus simply a fraction whose numerator is the number of favorable cases and whose denominator is the number of all possible cases. This statement explicitly defines the classical interpretation of probability.
